newsitem.title: USA: Colombia's Samper says political crisis is over.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper says political crisis is over.

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper said Wednesday that the political crisis surrounding his administration has ended and his country's economy would revive next year.

On the final day of a trip to New York, Samper told Reuters Financial Television that the Colombian economy had not suffered from allegations that the president knowingly accepted campaign contributions in 1994 from drug traffickers.
"The political crisis is over," Samper said. "It finished when the congress exonerated my behavior on any charge."
The Colombian Congress cleared the president in June of complicity in drug corruption, but this verdict failed to clear the issue for many citizens.

Business leaders and politicians, including former vice President Humberto de la Calle who stepped down earlier this month, have pressed Samper to resign, but the president has steadfastly maintained his innocence.
Samper said that Colombia's business community was far more concerned about the health of financial markets, the curbing of demand, and the lowering of interest rates.
"We will see a diminished growth rate this year, but I am totally confident that in January we will see a recovery of our economy," he said.
The Colombian government projected the gross domestic product will grow by 3.5 percent in 1996, well off the five percent pace of last year.
International investors have maintained faith in the economy, evidenced by the country's ability to sell its bonds at the height of the crisis, the president said.

The recent strength of the Colombian peso also may offer proof of domestic confidence in the economy, although diminished imports and the government crackdown on drug trafficking may also play roles, Samper said.
The guerrilla insurgency that has torn at the country should not have a destabilizing effect on the economy, the president said.

"For more than 40 years we have been accustomed to guerrilla operations," Samper said. "I have more than 25 percent of the armed forces used exclusively to protect the more sensitive economic points in the country."

The president said he has been considering candidates to replaces two members of the monetary board whose terms will expire in February 1997. "I can assure that I will seek the best names that I have in my economic team," he said.

The Clinton administration revoked Samper's visa to the United States because of the campaign contribution allegations, but the travel restriction do not apply to a head of state visiting the United Nations.
In a Monday address to the United Nations, Samper called for heightened international cooperation to battle the drug trade.-- 212-859-1671
